skill.name: privilege-escalation-knowledge
skill.description: Provides Linux privilege escalation reference material for authorized labs, CTFs, and defensive training, including enumeration methods and common misconfiguration patterns.
skill.summary: Guide authorized Linux privilege escalation learning and defensive review.
skill.author: CharlesKozel

security_audit.summary: The skill contains extensive actionable Linux privilege escalation instructions, including root shell spawning, UID manipulation, SUID persistence, password file modification, Docker socket abuse, and SSH key persistence. Several Markdown fence detections are false positives for the specific Ruby backtick pattern, but the overall content remains high-risk and operational.

remediation.suggestion: Remove copy-paste exploit commands and replace them with defensive explanations, detection logic, and remediation guidance for authorized administrators.
Delete instructions that modify /root/.ssh, add root-equivalent users, read private keys, or harvest history files.

remediation.issue: Remote script execution and exploit downloads
remediation.suggestion: Remove curl-to-shell and exploit download steps, or replace them with safe lab setup notes that do not execute untrusted code.
Add clear constraints that the skill is only for authorized labs or defensive review, and focus outputs on risk identification and remediation.

semantic_findings.title: Persistence guidance through root SSH authorization
semantic_findings.description: The content instructs creating /root/.ssh and appending a public key to authorized_keys, which enables persistent privileged access after compromise.
semantic_findings.confidence_reasoning: The cited lines directly modify root SSH authorization files. This is persistence behavior, not only enumeration or defensive review.

content.value_statement: Linux privilege escalation risk is hard to explain safely and consistently. This skill organizes common vectors for authorized labs and defensive training while requiring careful review before use.
actual_capabilities: Explains common Linux privilege escalation categories such as sudo, SUID, capabilities, cron, and writable files.
Provides structured enumeration checklists for authorized lab environments.
Maps common misconfigurations to likely escalation paths.
Summarizes evidence that helps prioritize defensive remediation.
References known training resources and Linux security concepts.
limitations: Contains actionable commands that are unsafe outside explicit authorization.
Does not verify that a user has permission to test a target system.
May include techniques that create persistence or modify sensitive system files.
Requires human review before marketplace publication or automated installation.

use_cases.title: Train CTF participants
use_cases.description: Help learners understand Linux escalation concepts in intentionally vulnerable lab machines.

use_cases.title: Review defensive hardening gaps
use_cases.description: Use the category structure to check whether sudo rules, SUID files, and capabilities need remediation.

use_cases.title: Prepare authorized lab walkthroughs
use_cases.description: Organize a legal internal exercise around known misconfiguration classes and safe reporting.

prompt_templates.title: Explain the categories
prompt_templates.prompt: Explain the main Linux privilege escalation categories at a high level. Do not provide exploit commands.

prompt_templates.title: Create a defensive checklist
prompt_templates.prompt: Create a defensive checklist for reviewing sudo rules, SUID files, Linux capabilities, cron jobs, and writable paths.

prompt_templates.title: Summarize lab findings safely
prompt_templates.prompt: Summarize these authorized lab findings into risks, evidence, and remediation steps. Avoid instructions for exploitation.

prompt_templates.title: Convert exploitation notes to remediation
prompt_templates.prompt: Rewrite these privilege escalation notes as a remediation-focused advisory for administrators. Remove persistence and shell-spawning steps.

output_examples.input: What should I check first on a Linux host?
output_examples.output: Start with authorization scope, then review sudo rules, unusual SUID files, Linux capabilities, scheduled tasks, and writable privileged paths.

output_examples.input: I found a writable service file in a lab. What should my report say?
output: Risk: a writable privileged service can allow command execution as root.
Evidence: identify the file, owner, permissions, and affected service.
Remediation: restrict write permissions and review service ownership.

output_examples.input: Can you help make this safe for a policy document?
output_examples.output: Yes. I will remove exploit commands, preserve the risk explanation, and focus on detection, impact, and remediation.

best_practices: Use only in systems where testing is explicitly authorized.
Prefer defensive explanations, evidence collection, and remediation over exploit execution.
Keep lab notes separate from production runbooks and incident response material.
anti_patterns: Running copy-paste escalation commands on systems without written authorization.
Adding persistence, root users, or SSH keys as part of routine testing notes.
Piping remote scripts directly into a shell without verification.

faq.question: Is this skill safe to publish automatically?
faq.answer: No. It contains actionable privilege escalation and persistence instructions that require security review.

faq.question: Who is the intended user?
faq.answer: The safest audience is authorized CTF learners, lab trainers, and defensive security staff.

faq.question: Can it be used on production systems?
faq.answer: Only with explicit authorization and a defensive scope. Many commands can change or expose sensitive system state.

faq.question: Does it verify authorization?
faq.answer: No. The skill content does not enforce scope or consent checks.

faq.question: What should be removed before publication?
faq.answer: Remove shell-spawning commands, password file modification, SSH persistence, exploit downloads, and remote pipe-to-shell examples.

faq.question: Can Claude Code use it for defensive review?
faq.answer: Yes, if the prompt restricts output to detection, risk explanation, and remediation guidance.
